p: Uh, do you get a high rate of complaints from a lot of the RAD/PACT developments?

I would not say there's a high rate of complaints. We certainly get complaints, but again, about 77% of the people who've been surveyed are satisfied. Um, I'll also note that CHPC recently did a study and looking at violations, and they concluded that the PACT program outperforms the resolution of violations, uh, as it relates to and compared to other forms of multifamily housing.

Okay. Okay, I'm gonna come back, uh, to my line of questioning. I'm actually

now gonna turn it over to, uh, Council Member Marte, who has some questions. Council Member Marte.

Thank you, uh, Chair Banks, and I wanna plus one, say, any data relevant to Fulton Chelsea Elliott Houses, we will love to have. It seems like there has been a lack of transparency for years. Um, not in this administration, I know it was in the previous administration, but we need to play catch-up and really find out what's happening there. Uh, my first question is, how much money does, uh, NYCHA spend on marketing for RAD and PACT and the Trust?
To my knowledge, we do not have a formal marketing budget for PACT, and NYCHA does not manage the Trust budget.

So when you go to developments, um, you know, I've seen you recently at Seward Park Extension, um, what is that orchestrated marketing event? Where can we see that in your line item? Is that personal staffers? Do you hire an outside contractor to create the presentations, to talk to the residents?

The vast majority of those people who go to the meetings and their engagement meetings, um, it's not marketing, it's really engagement, um, as I described before. And they— most of those folks come from the real estate team. There are some people within the COO's office as well who attend.

And, you know, there's been a lot of questions about surveys, and you mentioned it, uh, that you look to surveys to get residents' feedback. I know in the past there's been some misinformation of whether something is a survey or something is a vote. Is NYCHA willing to post a lot of the descriptions of these surveys online and classify which - also, are they willing to post what ballots look like online so the public can understand what is being put in front of these residents before they actually do a vote or they fill out a survey?

I mean, yes, we, we've been doing the surveys that I mentioned. These are, uh, surveys about the experience of going through the construction and then satisfaction after construction. Um, they are surveys, they are

described as surveys, and we have not posted them yet, but as we get a body of data, we will post them.

Yeah, because I think, you know, satisfaction is a— it's pretty broad terminology, right? You can do the survey the day after someone moves into a conversion, but that perception of satisfaction could drastically change 3 months or 6 months later. You know, as Chair Banks has mentioned, and I have seen personally is after 6 months, some of these buildings and apartments start falling apart, and it seems like it was all facade repair instead of really trying to change the lived experience for the long term. And so that's why, you know, we're asking for this data. We're asking for more transparency because you can say you got 70-somewhat percent satisfaction, but we don't know what the data is behind that narrative. And I think that narrative is used sometimes dangerously to convince other tenants of other developments to move to vote for a RAD/PACT, uh, conversion. Um, I'm gonna move, uh, my questioning to allocation from the Council to NYCHA. How much

allocation in the past 2 years has the Council done, uh, to NYCHA for capital repairs?
Sorry, one second.
Stop the clock, stop the clock, while you're searching because I want to give my colleague enough time to-

Um, thank you for the question, Council Member. So currently we have from the Council, um, $47 million, uh, across all active projects. So that's not in the last 2 years alone that have been allocated. Those projects could already be in construction. They could be recently allocated in planning, but that's the total funding we have across about 60 projects.
And how quickly is that funding used on average after the allocation from a Council Member?

Sure. Um, so a typical capital project can range, um, typically 4 to 5 years, um, from the allocation, the initial engagement with residents, the planning, the design, the procurement process, and construction. So it's typically a 4 to 5 year cycle, um, where we use city funding, including Council funding. That

is a little bit longer because of the city approvals that are involved, as opposed to our state or federal funding. In the last 5 years, uh, we've completed about 100 council-funded projects. Um, and so the 47, um, that we— sorry, the 60 or so that we have currently, as I said, they're in different phases, but, um, you know, would be completing— if they're already in construction, they'd be completing in the next 12 months or so. If they're back in the design phase, it's going to be several years before that, that, that asset gets delivered.
And can you talk about the range of investments that have been used with Council funding? So for example, roof repairs, benches, mailboxes, anything else?

Sure, the Council funding in particular, um, is a small portion of our overall budget, uh, as well as a small portion of our city allocations in terms of mayoral and agreement funding. The Council funding is typically targeted at obviously, um, items that residents have engaged with Council Members as being their priorities, but that fall within the allocation limit that's

available. So they are typically, as you mentioned, um, things like lobbies and mailboxes, playgrounds, community centers, lighting, CCTV cameras are probably our most common, um, types of funded projects. However, you know, Council Members may also, ah, opt to allocate to, um, other infrastructure repairs we're doing. Um, if we have other funding, they may supplement that. So even if it's a priority at a development, um, potentially contributing to a project that focuses on something like, you know, plumbing issues or, um, areas like that.

You know, it was really disturbing to hear from my budget director earlier this year that, this year, NYCHA is only allowing Council Members to fund security projects with capital funding. Um, have you changed it? First of all, why are you only allowing us to repair doors and cameras? Instead of roofs and other critical needs that NYCHA has?

Yeah, thank you for the question. I just heard this yesterday, in fact, and, um, there seems to be some type of miscommunication or misunderstanding. We do not currently, nor have we

ever, restricted, um, what Council Members can fund, and we're very happy with any type of allocations Council Members make. Um, so I'm not sure where that information came from, but on our side, there's no change in our policies. We provide to Council Members extensive guidance on all different types of projects they can fund, what the unit cost would be, how they could come up with a budget and work with us on a cost estimate. And that's a continual process that we're engaged in even recently with certain Council Members. Um, so if, um, you know, we, we'd love to talk more afterwards to correct whatever the misunderstanding might be.

Yeah, it would be great if you can send a memo Council-wide because it was a discussion among many Council Members of the restriction that we thought NYCHA was putting on, on our budget allocation. Uh, my final question, um, is about the City of Yes investment. You know, there was a $5 billion investment when it comes to City of Yes for all housing needs. Sadly, only $175 million of that was allocated to NYCHA. Um, how much of that money has

been spent so far, and can you break down, uh, what the uses are with those $170 million?

Thank you for that question, Council Member Marte. As of the Fiscal Year '27 Preliminary plan, as you noted, there's $175 million in capital investments for the City of Yes program. Um, that includes funding for repairs for vacant units, critical infrastructure, and environmental hazard mitigation. OMB, NYCHA, and City Hall are still working through the exact allocation of these funds. I can say that of the $175 million, $40 million was previously allocated for the Gowanus rezoning, asbestos and vacant units, and the ventilation damper project. There are also plans to reallocate an additional $71 million in additional asbestos abatement for vacant units and other capital projects, and that leaves us with an additional $63 million in unallocated capital, which we're still working through.
Wait, so, sorry Chair, just one more question.
Sure.

So you mentioned the Gowanus rezoning, which from my understanding, that was a separate negotiation that Council Member at the time, Brad Lander, had with the administration as part of the Gowanus rezoning. It seems like there's a double dip right now where you're using City of Yes committed allocation to fund something that should have already been funded in the past.

So before the City of Yes program, you are correct that there was $40 million that rolled over from the 2025 adopted plan, and this was used for Gowanus rezoning. That's only $12 million, in addition to $8 million for asbestos abatement for our vacant units, and, uh, also a ventilation damper project of $20 million.

It would be great to have a chart, a spreadsheet that shows rezoning commitment allocation, how much of that money has been used, because my fear, and my fear across agencies is that typically when we strike a deal, there's a lot of double dipping, and it kind of gives, you know, the Council a false pretense that we are giving you new money or negotiating new money for these agencies. But whenever we come to these oversight hearings, it

seems like some of the previous agreements are used, uh, in other agreements as well. And so it would be great to have transparency on not just the Gowanus rezoning, but any other rezoning that has happened where NYCHA is still using those funds to do capital investments.
Thank you.

Thank you. Well, we've been also joined by Council Member Epstein, and then now we'll move to Councilman Chi Ossé for questions. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: Thank you Chair, and good morning, folks. Uh, thank you for, uh, clarifying some of the misinformation that was being spread around the rental ripoff hearings. I know that those were open to NYCHA residents as well. If folks want to attend, I think there's another one on Saturday in East Harlem from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. So, uh, please show up and make sure that you are receiving, you know, in-person services from NYCHA if you have yet to go to a rental ripoff hearing. Uh, I wanna ask some questions in regards to a development within my district, uh, in Bed-Stuy. Tompkins Houses, more specifically 960 Park Avenue, has had a gas outage for the last 3 to 4 months and a rodent

issue at 808 Park Avenue in the Marcy development. The NYCHA representative who my office has been in contact with, uh, has not provided my office with a completion date. This issue of incomplete and unanswered capital and infrastructure work is common in my district, as I'm sure it is for my colleagues. Repairs take a long time or are half completed. With both a federal deficit and a city deficit, I'm concerned with how critical repairs will be addressed. You just answered Council Member Marte's question that there is an outstanding, uh, you know, amount of funds that were received from the City of Yes, I would like to advocate for my district for those funds to be allocated for this development. Could I get that commitment from you all today?

We are happy to work with our partners at OMB and City Hall on that commitment, um, but I cannot confirm today that that's how those funds would be used. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: Okay, so how can we guarantee that despite these deficits that NYCHA will be responsive and address all needed repairs, including the ones at Tompkins and Marcy Houses?

Thank you Council Member, for those questions. I will definitely be following up with your office directly, uh, on these two issues for both Marcy and Tompkins. As you know, gas outages are a matter of public health, and they require coordination with many city, city and other agency partners like the utilities, so they can take a long time to be complete. We do follow the requirements to have lobby meetings, uh, with residents to keep them updated on that. So I apologize if your office hasn't been kept in the loop, but we will follow up on both that and the rodent issue at Marcy. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: Thank you. I do wanna follow up on some questions around PACT/RAD. Is there a consistent evaluation process in regards to repairs, maintenance, conditions, etcetera, after the PACT/RAD transition?

During the construction process, uh, we have a team of folks, both NYCHA employees within the the real estate group, um, and also some folks within the compliance team, as well as, uh, a third-party, uh, construction manager who goes out throughout the construction process to

ensure that the scope of work is being executed as we anticipated and is in our agreements. So we go through that whole process and then when we get closer to the end of the construction process, we tour the site with our PACT partner, um, to verify it. We go through and we make sure that everything is to our satisfaction. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: I think NYCHA should set up consistent meetings with both private managements at PACT Developments as well as relevant city agencies as well as members of, of the City Council just to keep all of us updated on progress when it comes to what happens after that transition. I think because this is such a controversial, uh, you know, thing that happens within our public housing system, I think keeping all active partners on the same page in terms of how things are progressing is really important. My office is very responsive, always open to hearing updates about different changes that are happening within our district. I think a consistent communication both from the private developer facilitated by NYCHA would be really helpful in those

cases. Is that something that we can expect with this administration?

Yes, thank you. That's a great suggestion. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: Thank you. Uh, how can enforcement measures, especially in light of budget deficits, be more robust if private management has been terrible in those RAD/PACT conversions?

Well, we have the right, uh, within all of our agreements to remove, uh, the property manager. Uh, our goal is to hopefully never get there. So again, we are working with our property managers on a daily basis through the asset management team, the compliance team, etcetera and really in making sure that things are working as they should. Obviously issues do come up and we work to rectify them as quickly as possible. And we've only had, uh, 2 instances where we've switched out property managers. COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: Thank you. Um, I wanna speak about potential federal cuts or, uh, additional federal cuts. In past budget negotiations, the federal administration has threatened to, as you've

laid out in your testimony, make cuts to NYCHA. And for example, according to the Independent Budget Office's report this past fall, the federal government proposed a $27 billion reduction in public housing nationwide. Uh, does NYCHA have a plan on how they would address funding cuts if the federal administration proceeds with more cuts in future budget negotiations?

Thank you for that question, Council Member Ossé. As you mentioned, um, we are in fact currently dealing with a potential reduction of $789 million nationwide, which is around 14%. It could be at least $100 million for NYCHA. Currently, we are still working with HUD to determine our final eligibility for funds, so we're happy to come back to the Council in May once those conversations with HUD have been completed to give you a more fulsome answer. But we do have contingency plans in place, and of course we'll try our best to ensure that we continue to manage life, health, and safety, um, systems and processes for our residents.

COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: Thank you very much. Thank you so much, Chair, for the opportunity to ask questions, and I'm looking forward to hearing some follow-up on some of the questions.

Okay, thank you. Uh, we're now moving on to, uh, Council Member Encarnación. Elsie. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: There you go. Hello everyone. Um, you know, I'm gonna be honest, I, I— outside of the Committee that I Chair, this is the only other Committee that I have multiple pages of questions for. Um, I have 23 developments in my district, the most in the whole country, I believe. Um, so this is extremely important to me, and I'm very grateful to the other Council Members who have asked some of the questions that I had. Um, in terms of the RAD/PACT; so I'm gonna jump around a little bit to try to hit a little bit of everything, but in terms of the RAD/PACT, during the transition time, uh, a lot of the constituents that we serve have been getting a lot of runaround. Either they're going to NYCHA, they're going to the new management office that usually has someone in development on site, um, being told that, you know,

uh, tickets are not being answered because they're- they're in this weird transition phase, and we're trying to get a handle on how to direct them. So during a transition phase for RAD/PACT, who is responsible before the closing? Can we just be clear about who is responsible for repairs, who is responsible for the residents?

So right up until the closing or the conversion, it is still a NYCHA managed property. So all repairs, all tickets, all of that still should go through NYCHA and then once we've converted, the new property manager takes over. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: Okay and, um, I wanted to now switch over to a boiler explosion that happened in my district over at the Mitchell Houses, um, in the Bronx. I want to understand how NYCHA is prioritizing funding for gas line inspections, boiler inspections, and that sort. I mean, that miraculously there was no life, life lost there, but it- it could have ended very differently and the people in that community are still suffering. I do want to say that NYCHA was there. They were there for a very long time helping

get us on, on, uh, track as early as possible. But I just— I'm very fearful that it will happen again.

Thank you, Council Member. Yes, we're all very grateful that that morning did not result in any loss of life. Um, we are working closely with Department of Buildings and Department of Investigation, who are leading the investigation into the root cause of that incident to define exactly what caused that explosion that morning. However, I'm very pleased to say that gas has been restored to all the buildings in Mitchell as of last Friday. The last building went on. However, we had been restoring buildings, uh, one at a time, uh, starting with the first building that came online just 25 days after the explosion. So, um, all residents now have gas. We were also able to bring heat and hot water up at the development within days. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: I, I understand, and I don't mean to cut you off about Mitchell. I just want to understand the prioritization method by which, uh, NYCHA is looking at the portfolio, which buildings get prioritized in terms of inspections.

So all, all of our boilers and heating systems are required to go through Department of Buildings inspections, and so we are, we are in compliance with that. We work closely with the Department of Buildings. We do our summer overhaul, which we've actually already started now on some of our warmer days, to make sure our— all of our heating system is, is inspected and reviewed. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: Okay and you know, some of my developments in the district continue to have consistent unsanitary trash pileups despite the new garbage bin installation. Some of my staff recently saw trash bags and litter on top of the awnings, on top of— I mean, it's just everywhere. What further steps is NYCHA taking to address consistently low quality of sanitary conditions in the developments? And are there benchmarks for success in this area?

Thank you, Council Member. I'd also like to encourage you— I know you probably work very closely with Brian Honan every day— but as you have specific instances, to please let us know so that we can follow up right away on those conditions. We definitely don't want trash sitting out. We know

that it causes pests. Overall, we've had, uh, you know, we're working with sanitation on all of our trash collections. Obviously, due to the snowstorms, there were delays in trash collections all over the city, not just for NYCHA. But if you have specific instances where you are seeing that, we're happy to follow up. I also wanna say regarding trash on canopies, that is an ongoing challenge for NYCHA. It's something we are focused on across all of our developments. Um, we did issue a new policy last year around uh, trash for residents to try to cut down on what we call window littering. And, uh, we have, uh, told residents that we would start imposing fines if we are able to, um, confirm that they, uh, committed window littering. So we are trying our best to educate residents on that issue to try to cut that down. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: Yeah, I mean, I don't know how much the fines will work. I mean, if we're not able to collect rent, we're not going to collect fines, so.

But we're- we're trying our best to at least let them know that this is a requirement of their lease to not conduct those types of behaviors. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: And in light of the proposed federal guidance from the US Department of Housing and Urban Development that could restrict mixed status or immigrant households from accessing federal housing assistance, how is NYCHA prepared, uh, to respond to this? Uh, are— do you have any policies or protections being considered to prevent the displacement or loss of housing for those affected families?

Thank you so much for that question. Uh, for those of you who don't know, HUD released a new proposed rule regarding mandatory recertification of eligible status families on February 20th. NYCHA values all residents who live in our public housing and Section 8 portfolios, and we are deeply concerned about any proposal that might separate families or that would lead to eviction. We're currently examining the impact of the proposed rule, and we're working diligently both internally and externally with our city partners, uh, to respond to, uh, the comment on the proposed rule

change, uh, that's due at the end of April. Um, and we'll be happy to share, uh, once we have, um, a greater idea of how we're going to, uh, respond to the rule. However, the greatest challenge for us is that we are basically fully funded by HUD, and we are required to follow, uh, the regulations that are proposed and enacted by the federal government, as awful as they seem. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: Okay. Well, I look forward to that document and I also look forward to the document about us being able to use our funding for something outside of security. Uh, because I— we, we heard the same thing on our end.

Thank you. Uh, we've been joined by, uh, Chair of Finance, Council Member Lee, and we'll now proceed to, uh, Council Member Avilés with questions. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Oh, thank you. Thank you, Chair. Good afternoon, NYCHA team. Um, so I'm going to jump in because I don't want to waste time. Um, I'd like to talk about vacant unit readiness, my favorite topic, given that we are in a housing crisis and we still have thousands of apartments sitting

empty. So let's- let's understand what's happening here. So the PMMR reports that the median number of days for vacant unit readiness was 350.1 for the first 4 months of 2026. While this shows a decreasing trend over the last 2 years, the turnaround time is still well above 300 days. Are there operational or administrative challenges that cause the delays in vacant unit readiness turnaround times?

Thank you, Council Member. Um, I know we have, uh, talked, uh, extensively about this issue before. Um, so I do wanna report that our current turnaround time, uh, for vacant units is down to 341 days as of February 2025. Uh, and that's down from 401 days the previous February. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Can you say that one more closer to the mic?

341 days as of February 2026, sorry. And that's down from 401 days in February 2025. We are- so we are moving in the right direction towards our goal of 300 days and that's what's most important is that trajectory. We continue to look at ways to increase productivity. And again, as we address the longest standing vacant

units, that turnaround time obviously stays, stays very long. But the more we get to sooner units, that turnaround time will come down. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: So what are, what are the specific problems?

Yeah I just wanna add that, um, in 2025, we turned over the highest number in recent years with 4,703 move-ins in 2025, which is a 76% increase since 2023. But so what is the total number that exists right now, vacant units?

So right now our vacant units that are in the turnover process are 6,192, and that's as of March 1st. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Okay, given- given obviously there is improvement, we gotta give that credit, but we're still, well, we're almost still a year to turn over apartments. We're still above 6,000 empty units. What is going— what, what are the problems that we can't seem to get at?

So again, the- the major causes of the turnaround time are the environmental work that we think is very important, um, and also required to, to happen as part of turnover.

So both lead and asbestos work is performed in every unit upon turnover. It, you know, we have the testing information if they are found to have those hazards. They are made, uh, full lead abatement. So, you know, fully cleared of lead and asbestos-free. So we have to do— go through that environmental process before we start any of the regular skilled trades work. And again, it's important to remember that our residents are typically in those apartments for about 27 years. So there's significant skilled trade work that's needed. Um, typically we take out all of the cabinets, we put in new plumbing fixtures, um, plastering and painting all has to happen in the apartment before it's even ready to be shown for a selected and prospective tenant. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: So how many contracts do we have related to lead and asbestos? Like, where are the problems? Do we have not enough contractors? Do we have not enough, uh, employees? Like, where are the problems here?

Uh, one other issue that we face in seeing a total reduction is that, again, 60% of our move-ins are actually transfers. So for 60% of the

time when we move someone in, we are creating another vacant unit. And so that does prevent us from seeing a total decrease. But I think the important thing is that increase in production that we're seeing year over year is showing that we're getting through those blockades, that we're, that we're able to provide healthy, environmentally cleaned apartments for new prospective tenants is very important. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: So how much have we invested in contracts for lead and asbestos, uh, abatement?

On— so on, uh, rather than focus on the contract amount, I'd say for per unit for lead abatement for a turnover is about $20,000, and for asbestos it's about $25,000 per unit. That's just for the environmental work. Our expense cost, if we do most of our unit turnovers in-house through skilled trade overtime, and that's about $16,000 per unit. And so we- we're averaging, I'd say, in a full environmental, if both hazards are there, uh, we're looking at about $40,000 per unit. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: So even, even with some, I, yeah, I, do you wanna, do you wanna respond?

Okay, I, I just gotta say, like, even with— I— so obviously there are— we have seen multiple, uh, variations of how much it's costing to turn over an apartment. Even at $50,000 or $60,000 per apartment, the city has invested quite a lot of money. Well over— if you, if you just did the dirty math of $60,000 per apartment and 6,000 apartments, the city itself has invested well above and beyond the cost of what that would be. So we seem to have an ongoing problem of continued large investments in capital, costs that don't add up, and a pool of apartments that we can't seem to get online. So we really want to be able to figure out how to drill down and, and get over this hump that we've been talking about for 4 years, um, which I'm sure persisted well before our tenure. But I— while there's some progress, I— the math doesn't math, and we still have thousands of apartments sitting around campuses. And in Red Hook alone, we have over 200 empty apartments. I, I, I'm mystified. Ah, I— we keep having the same conversation. It's a little bit like Groundhog's Day. I compliment you for decreasing a couple of days, and yet we have this incredible pool

of apartments sitting available, people waiting for years to get transfers, living with their abusers. Now we have the Trump Administration coming for immigrant families. We have people who are on the brink of homelessness, people who have to go to shelter because an apartment can't come online. What is going to give here?

As I've said, we, uh, I think the production numbers speak for themselves. We are doing more move-ins than we ever have in recent times in— because we recognize that this is an extremely important affordable housing. However, in addition to the city money, which we're very grateful for, we are using our own federal funds as well for these turnovers. It is more, um, there is more funding needed and so we use our overtime, as I said, in order to support this effort as well. So we are putting everything we have towards these turnovers, but with— because we recognize transfers are a very needy cause as well. Residents need to be able to, um, you know, escape abusers, to move into conditions that are better than where they are now.

So we do have to facilitate emergency transfers, and that is 60% of those move-ins. So yes, it is hard to see an overall number decrease when we are doing that level of transfers.
Alright - COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Chair, if, if I could, I just read through questions that not— and, and have NYCHA return, uh,
You can, you can do that during the second round. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Okay, I gotta go.
If you wanna wait till the second round. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: It’s okay.
We can- I'd be happy to— set up a follow-up.
Thank you. Unless you wanna give them to another Council Member. Council Member Epstein, thank you.

Thank you, Chair and, uh, thank you, NYCHA. So can we require a vote of residents at future RAD/PACT, uh, conversions? So residents actually have a say in future RAD/PACT conversions? It's a yes/no. It's really simple.
Yeah, I just was trying, trying to get—
Yeah, thank you.
Thank you for the question. No.

Okay, so, uh, I really think it's a problem, to be honest and I know I don't want to get on my high horse, but when residents aren't engaged in this process, they don't really understand what their impact is and I want to flag this for NYCHA. I know there's state legislation pending, and I also in a prior life had state legislation. I would encourage you to reconsider that position. First Houses, uh, spent a long time, uh, spent— the people have been out of their homes for 2 years. When are you going to commit to moving all the residents back into First Houses by?

Thank you, Council Member. As you know, I attended every quarterly meeting at First Houses as part of the roof reconstruction project. We have almost completed all of the move-ins, so we expect they will be completed very soon.

Many residents, uh, opted to stay in their relocated apartments. Um, so, uh, we think we only have a handful, but I'm happy to follow up with you.
Yeah, I'd like to know by when, because they keep asking me. I see them on the street, they want to move home. So we agreed to move them out and be back in 18 months. It's been over 2 years.

We're finishing the fi— the final— the residents weren't relocated for 2 years. The first phase started 2 years ago, but for the final phase, there are a handful of residents still waiting to have those apartments finalized, and then they can make their options.
So I'd love to have a date.
Absolutely, we'll send it.

Thank you. And we talk a lot about greening New York City, and NYCHA obviously, how do we get NYCHA to start moving forward in our, you know, the state laws, CLCPA requires us to move for more environmental sustainability. Can we get NYCHA to start composting?

Thank you for the question, uh, Council Member. So we have, um, run a number of, um, composting pilots in the past. Uh, we've also, uh, worked with Green City Force who runs farms at some of our sites and have a composting operation. And so, um, you know, we are always, uh, open to, uh, funding opportunities that allow us to expand those efforts that have been successful to date.
So the answer wasn't really an answer. So when can we get NYCHA to start composting?
So we're doing it at a limited scale.

It's required across the city. Every tenant in New York City except people who live in public housing has an obligation to compost.
